The function repeats: add whole periods, 2π for sine and cosine, π for tangent
Divide numerator and denominator by the highest power of the denominator
Get the trigonometric function on its own
Inside one period the solution is one interval or two, found from the inverse function; every period gives the same ones again, 2kπ later (kπ for tangent and cotangent)
Now the inside is x: subtract and divide on every part
Sine and cosine are always between −1 and 1
Every term has degree 2: divide by x² and write t = y/x (x = 0 is no solution of this equation, it is checked on its own)
The inside of |…| is positive or negative: |g| is g where g ≥ 0 and −g where g < 0. Each case is an equation of its own
Solve this case: its solutions only count where its condition holds
Each inequality is solved on its own first
All of them have to hold: only the values that are in every solution are left
Logarithms to the same base: a sum is the logarithm of the product, a difference the logarithm of the quotient, and n·log a is log(aⁿ)
ln a / ln b is the logarithm of a to the base b (change of base)
√a − b is ∞ − ∞ here: multiplying by the conjugate (the same with the other sign) turns it into a quotient
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²: the roots disappear from the numerator
If the exponent goes to ∞, eᵍ goes to ∞; if it goes to −∞, eᵍ goes to 0
Close to the point on this side the inside of |…| keeps its sign, so |g| = g (positive) or −g (negative)
Terms that go to 0 vanish (a variable in a denominator, e^(−x)), and arctan of a growing number is ±π/2
The limit of a constant is the constant
The highest power grows without bound
A denominator that grows without bound: the quotient goes to 0
Substitute u = 1/x: then u goes to 0
The base goes to 1 and the exponent to ∞: write the power with e and take the limit of the exponent
The limit is e to the power of that limit
Find the zeros of the polynomial (rational root theorem): each zero r gives a factor (x − r)
To use a matrix or vector again, store it with := (long press on =), for example v := [vector]
The determinant of a 2×2 matrix: the product of the diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal
Expand the determinant along a row or column: each entry times the determinant of what is left when its row and column are crossed out, the signs alternate
The inverse of a 2×2 matrix: swap the diagonal, change the signs of the other two entries, and divide by the determinant
Write the matrix next to the identity matrix: row operations that turn the left part into the identity turn the right part into the inverse
Swap two rows to get a pivot that is not 0
Divide the row by its pivot so that the pivot is 1
Add or subtract a multiple of the pivot row to make the other entries in this column 0
Row reduction: row operations turn every pivot into 1 and the other entries in its column into 0 (reduced row echelon form)
The eigenvalues λ are where A − λ·I is not invertible: the determinant of A − λ·I is 0
An eigenvector v of this eigenvalue solves (A − λ·I)·v = 0: reduce the rows
Free variables are set to 1 and 0; v is scaled to whole numbers (any multiple is an eigenvector as well)
The eigenvalues, each with an eigenvector
The left part is the identity matrix: the right part is the inverse
Multiply the matrices: each entry is a row of the first times a column of the second
A number times a matrix: it multiplies every entry
Add the matrices entry by entry
Subtract the matrices entry by entry
A power of a matrix is the matrix multiplied by itself
One bound is infinite: the antiderivative at t instead of at the bound, and the limit as t goes to infinity
The denominator goes to 0 and the numerator does not: the quotient grows without bound, the signs say which way
The logarithm of a number that goes to 0⁺ goes to −∞
It is 0·∞: write the product as a quotient first
It is 0/0 or ∞/∞: apply l\'Hôpital\'s rule
A fraction is zero if its numerator is zero
Two absolute values are equal: the insides are equal or opposite
Split into the two cases of the absolute value
Raise the base to the power of both sides

SI: m, kg, m³, N, Pa, J, K, …
US: ft, lb, US gal, psi, …
Middle value when sorted; for an even count the mean of the two middle ones
Spread of a sample drawn from a larger population, divides by n − 1
Spread of a complete population, divides by n
Square of the sample standard deviation, divides by n − 1
Square of the population standard deviation, divides by n
s/√n: how precisely a sample\'s mean estimates the population mean
Ways to choose k of n items, order does not matter: nCr(n, k)
Ways to arrange k of n items in order: nPr(n, k)
Largest whole number dividing all values
Smallest positive multiple of all values
To the nearest whole number, halves away from zero
round(x, n): x with n decimal places
Largest whole number not above the value
Smallest whole number not below the value
Most frequent value; the first of them if several occur equally often
Adds up the values you list: sum(2, 4, 9) = 15. For a series with an index running from a lower to an upper bound use the Σ key
Multiplies the values you list: prod(2, 4, 9) = 72. For a series with an index running from a lower to an upper bound use the ∏ key (long press Σ)
The squares of the values added up: sumsq(1, 2, 3) = 14
percentile(p, values…): the value below which p percent (0 to 100) of the data lie, interpolated between neighbours
quartile(q, values…): q from 0 to 4, where 2 is the median
Asymmetry of the data (population): 0 if symmetric, positive if the long tail is on the right. Needs at least 3 values
Margin of error of the mean (t)
tmargin(c, values…): the margin of error t·s/√n of the confidence interval of level c (0.95 for 95%) for the mean, with t = tinv((1 + c)/2, n − 1). The interval is mean ± margin
tstat(μ₀, values…): (mean − μ₀)/(s/√n), the statistic of a one-sample t test against μ₀. Compare it with tinv or work out the p-value with tcdf
Ways to split k₁ + k₂ + … items into groups of these sizes
totient(n): how many of 1…n have no common factor with n. For whole numbers; one with only very large prime factors can take too long

factor(n): n as a product of prime powers, e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Shown as a product when factor(n) is the whole line. Numbers with only large prime factors can take too long. Decimal, Hex etc. show the number itself
expand(e): products and powers of sums multiplied out, e.g. (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1

apart(e): a fraction of polynomials as a polynomial plus partial fractions, e.g. 1/(x² − 1) = ½/(x − 1) − ½/(x + 1). The denominator must split into factors x − r with rational r, and at most one quadratic without rational roots (x² + 1). One variable

taylor(f, n), taylor(f, x, n) or taylor(f, x, a, n): the Taylor polynomial of f in x around a (0 if left out) up to the power n, e.g. taylor(sin(x), x, 0, 5) = x − x³/6 + x⁵/120. n up to 12. Written in powers of (x − a). Fails where f or a derivative is not defined at a (ln(x) at 0)
Write the equation in standard form
Multiply by μ: the left side is (μ·y)′. Integrate both sides
Separate the variables: everything with y on the left, everything with x on the right
Try y = eʳˣ: this gives the characteristic equation
General solution of the equation without the right side: for two real roots C₁·eʳ¹ˣ + C₂·eʳ²ˣ, for a double root (C₁ + C₂·x)·eʳˣ, for complex roots α ± βi: eᵃˣ·(C₁·cos(βx) + C₂·sin(βx))
Find a particular solution by variation of parameters (W is the Wronskian)
Choose the constants so that the initial conditions hold

dsolve(equation) or dsolve(equation, x₀, y₀): solves an ordinary differential equation typed with the derivative key, e.g. dsolve(d/dx(y) = 2x·y) gives y = C·e^(x²). First order: linear or separable. Second order (also dsolve(equation, x₀, y₀, y′₀)): a·y″ + b·y′ + c·y = r(x) with numbers a, b, c. The solution is checked in the equation; the constants are C (C₁, C₂). Not solved: other types, third order
modpow(b, e, m): bᵉ mod m without working out the huge power. A negative e needs b to have an inverse modulo m
√(a² + b² + …): hypot(3, 4) = 5. The length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle; for the length of a vector use norm
Cuts off the decimals (rounds towards zero); trunc(x, n) keeps n places
Decimals of x with the sign of x: frac(−2.75) = −0.75
−1, 0 or 1 for a negative number, zero or a positive number
The real part a of a + b·i
The imaginary part b of a + b·i
The angle of the number to the positive real axis in radians, from −π (excluded) to π
Γ(x) continues the factorial to numbers that are not whole: Γ(n + 1) = n!. Exact for whole and half numbers
ln Γ(x) for x > 0; stays small where Γ(x) gets too large
ψ(x) = Γ\'(x)/Γ(x), the slope of ln Γ(x). It appears in the derivative of gamma
2/√π · ∫₀ˣ e^(−t²) dt, the basis of the normal distribution
1 − erf(x), also accurate for large x
gammainc(a, x): the regularized lower incomplete gamma function P(a, x) = γ(a, x)/Γ(a), for a > 0 and x ≥ 0. The chi-square distribution is chisqcdf(x, k) = gammainc(k/2, x/2)
betainc(x, a, b): the regularized incomplete beta function Iₓ(a, b), for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and a, b > 0. The cumulative binomial and Student t distributions are made of it
lambertw(x): the w ≥ −1 with w·eʷ = x, for x ≥ −1/e. The solution of x·eˣ = 5 is lambertw(5)
sinint(x) = Si(x) = ∫₀ˣ sin t / t dt. It is the result of ∫ sin x / x dx
cosint(x) = Ci(x) = γ + ln x + ∫₀ˣ (cos t − 1)/t dt, for x ≠ 0. It is the result of ∫ cos x / x dx
expint(x) = Ei(x) = the principal value of ∫ from −∞ to x of eᵗ/t dt, for x ≠ 0. It is the result of ∫ eˣ / x dx
normalpdf(x, μ, σ): the bell curve at x. Without μ and σ the standard normal distribution (μ = 0, σ = 1)
normalcdf(x, μ, σ): the probability of a value up to x. Without μ and σ the standard normal distribution
normalinv(p, μ, σ): the x with the probability p for a value up to it, for 0 < p < 1. Without μ and σ the standard normal distribution
binompdf(n, p, k): the probability of exactly k successes in n trials with a success probability p
binomcdf(n, p, k): the probability of at most k successes in n trials with a success probability p
poissonpdf(λ, k): the probability of exactly k events when λ are expected
poissoncdf(λ, k): the probability of at most k events when λ are expected
tpdf(x, df): the density of the t distribution with df degrees of freedom
tcdf(x, df): the probability of a value up to x in the t distribution with df degrees of freedom
tinv(p, df): the x with the probability p for a value up to it, for 0 < p < 1. Gives the critical values of confidence intervals and t tests
chisqpdf(x, df): the density of the chi-square distribution with df degrees of freedom
chisqcdf(x, df): the probability of a value up to x in the chi-square distribution with df degrees of freedom
chisqinv(p, df): the x with the probability p for a value up to it, for 0 < p < 1. Gives the critical values of chi-square tests
rand(): a random number from 0 up to (not including) 1. It is drawn once per line: it stays the same while you edit the line, and it is kept with the result in the history
randint(a, b): a random whole number from a to b, both included. Drawn once per line, like rand()
randnorm(μ, σ): a random number of the normal distribution; without μ and σ the standard one (μ = 0, σ = 1). Drawn once per line
dot(a, b) = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + …, a number. Enter the vectors with the matrix key, as one column (or one row)
cross(a, b): the vector perpendicular to a and b (3 components each); its length is |a|·|b|·sin θ
norm(a) = √(a₁² + a₂² + …). The bars |a| give the same
angle(a, b) = acos(a·b / (|a|·|b|)), in the unit of the angle setting
proj(a, b): the part of a in the direction of b, (a·b)/(b·b)·b
unitvec(a): the vector divided by its length, so it has length 1 and the same direction
